findings.quote: It may be riding the edge of the circle its chain allows, not dragging its sinker.
findings.note: PARTIALLY / WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick C (~70%). General marine knowledge of a moored buoy's watch circle points straight at C, and C is also the only qualified option ('may be') beside three assertive ones ('must be', 'for most of the year', 'will lift it'). The hedge asymmetry is a probabilistic test-wise tell rather than a determinative one and the distractors are substantive positions, so this routes to adjudication instead of a lethal verdict.

findings.quote: What keeping a floating light on station involves, and an unsettled argument about slack.
findings.note: PARTIALLY, blind pick B (~75%). Standard main-idea umbrella tell: B names both the process and a controversy while A, C and D each name one narrow thread (a lightship crew, logger advocacy, maintenance cost). Scope comparison alone answers it without the passage. Normal main-idea design, so flag rather than kill.

findings.quote: It builds up where the chain drags on the bottom and close to the swivel.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick B. Marine domain knowledge says mooring-chain wear concentrates in the touchdown zone and at the swivel, and that mechanical abrasion outweighs salt corrosion, which weakens C; A's universal per-link figure and D's channel-width rationale also read as informed-solver rejects. A, C and D are still substantive claims a passage could ground, so flag rather than kill.

findings.quote: It may be riding the edge of the circle its chain allows, not dragging its sinker.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick C, with a modal asymmetry alongside it: A says 'must be', D says 'will' and B generalises to 'most of the year', while C alone is hedged, and watch-circle swing is standard buoy knowledge. The distractors are real operational claims (A is even true in itself), so the form tell is not decisive on its own - flag, not kill.

findings.quote: Its mooring chain must be longer than the depth of the water it lies in.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: the option restates a rule the passage asserts outright -- 'A floating aid is fixed to nothing; it is moored, and a mooring has to be slack. Chain longer than the depth lets the buoy lift to a sea instead of being pulled under by it' -- with the worked figure 'thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water'. A candidate can therefore say the option is a true statement about the off-position buoy and cite the line in a complaint. It is beatable: the prompt asks what is IMPLIED by finding the buoy away from its charted place, and the slack-mooring rule is stated explicitly and holds equally for a buoy sitting exactly on its cross, so it distinguishes nothing and is not an inference from the observation. The key is the passage's own explanation of that observation -- 'wind and tide swing the buoy about its sinker, and the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over, so the light is somewhere inside that circle rather than on the cross printed on the chart' -- and it also carries the 'not dragging its sinker' contrast the key needs. Key remains clearly best; not a double key, flagged for adjudication as an attractive true-but-unresponsive option.

findings.quote: sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 5/house style: the piece otherwise spells out every measured quantity ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'about forty minutes'); this lone Arabic numeral breaks the established style. Editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places'.

findings.quote: through the spring floods, the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places
findings.note: class 3: collocation. In a tidal context the trade term is 'spring tides' (or 'at springs'); 'the spring floods' invites the seasonal snowmelt reading and an editor would pause. Editor's rewrite: 'through the spring tides, the buoys laid longest sit ...'.

findings.quote: as much as 35 metres from their charted places
findings.note: class 4 (house style / register coherence): every other measurement in the piece is spelled out ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'eleven fresh links'), and this lone figure breaks the pattern mid-argument; a copy editor would harmonise. editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places'.

findings.quote: sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 5/house style: the article spells out every other quantity ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'forty minutes'), then switches to figures for this one; a sub-editor would normalise. Editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places'.

findings.quote: through the spring floods
findings.note: class 3 idiom/collocation: in a coastal-buoy context the intended sense is the flood tide at springs, but bare 'the spring floods' reads as seasonal river flooding; an editor would query the ambiguity. Editor's rewrite: 'through the spring tides' or 'on the spring floods'.

findings.quote: through the spring floods, the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 3 idiom/collocation: 'the spring floods' is not the English term for the tidal state a mooring-swing figure would be quoted against. In British marine prose a 'flood' is the incoming tide and the periodic maximum is 'springs', so the tidal phrasing is 'at springs' / 'through the spring tides'; 'spring floods' reads as the Nordic snowmelt sense (varflod) carried into English. Editor's rewrite: 'through the spring tides, the buoys laid longest sit as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places for hours together'

findings.quote: as much as 35 metres
findings.note: class 5 house style: every other quantity in the piece is spelled out ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'forty minutes'), with numerals reserved for years and the buoy's number; this lone figure breaks the pattern. Editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres'

findings.quote: the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 5: numeral style breaks with the rest of the piece, which spells out every comparable quantity ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'about forty minutes'); a copy editor would regularise. Rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places'.

findings.quote: a lift, a scrape, a fresh lamp and a relay take about forty minutes
findings.note: class 3: 'a relay' used as a noun for re-laying the buoy collides with the ordinary sense of 'relay'; the trade spelling is hyphenated. Rewrite: 'a lift, a scrape, a fresh lamp and a re-lay take about forty minutes'.

findings.quote: through the spring floods, the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 3: 'spring floods' is not the phrase a British marine writer uses for what swings a moored buoy. An editor reads it either as river snowmelt (the Swedish 'varflod') or as a mangled 'spring tides'; the excursion driver at a sea buoy is the spring tidal stream, and the passage elsewhere keeps trade terms exact ('scope', 'sinker', 'swivel'). Editor's rewrite: 'through the spring tides, the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together'.

findings.quote: as much as 35 metres
findings.note: class 4: numeral style breaks the passage's own convention - every other measure is spelled out ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'about forty minutes'). Editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres'.

findings.quote: Tuning can cost more than the bronze on a small bell, and less than it on a heavy one.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick D (~70%). Tuning labour is roughly fixed per bell while metal cost scales with mass, so the cross-over D describes is the economically expected answer; A is D's absolute-form contradiction ('always takes a larger share'). The remaining distractors are substantive claims a passage would have to settle.

findings.quote: The bell has to leave the mould heavier, since the metal tuning removes must be there first.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick A (~80%). Bell tuning only ever removes metal, so a founder intending to tune all five partials tightly must cast heavy — ordinary founding knowledge decides this blind. D also falls to 'always'. Still a genuine comprehension question a passage would ground, hence flag not kill.

findings.quote: How a bell's partials are tuned, what that work costs, and how far founders take it.
findings.note: PARTIALLY, blind pick D (~85%). Main-idea umbrella tell: D semantically contains the other three, which are narrow (price driver), obscure (bronze recovery) or evaluative (deserve more care). Answerable by scope comparison with no passage.

findings.quote: Tuning can cost more than the bronze on a small bell, and less than it on a heavy one.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick D. Tuning labour scales with the number of partials rather than with mass while metal cost scales with mass, so an informed solver predicts the two-sided claim and discounts A ('always takes a larger share') and C (lathe time rising with weight) on the same reasoning. Distractors remain substantive positions, so flag.

findings.quote: The bell has to leave the mould heavier, since the metal tuning removes must be there first.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick A. Bell tuning is subtractive lathe work, so anyone who knows the craft infers the casting must carry surplus metal; B is additionally false in the world as stated ('Every partial in the bell is lowered by thinning'), and D carries 'always'. This is inference from domain knowledge rather than recall and the distractors are substantive, so flag.

findings.quote: Every partial in the bell is lowered by thinning the band of metal that governs it.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: the passage states this mechanism verbatim -- 'Each partial answers to a band of metal at a particular height inside the bell, and thinning that band pulls the partial down. Nothing pulls it back up.' A founder who tunes all five tightly does lower all five by thinning, so the option is true of him. It is beatable on two counts: the prompt asks what is IMPLIED about a founder who INTENDS tight tuning, and the mechanism is explicit and holds for every founder including Kunert, so it distinguishes nothing; and 'Every partial in the bell' overreaches past the five, since the text also names 'the upper partials' the ear assembles, which no one turns. The key's support is stronger and specific to the intent -- 'That one-way arrow is why founders cast heavy' plus 'carrying an allowance of metal -- twelve kilos on the Cawden bell, against a finished weight of two hundred and twenty-eight -- that exists only to be turned away' and 'They would meet it four kilos apart at the pour'. Not a double key; flagged as an attractive distractor for adjudication.

findings.quote: Every partial in the bell is lowered by thinning the band of metal that governs it.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: the mechanism is in the passage verbatim -- 'Each partial answers to a band of metal at a particular height inside the bell, and thinning that band pulls the partial down. Nothing pulls it back up.' -- so a founder who brings all five down does it by thinning, and a candidate could cite that line. It is beatable twice over: the prompt asks what is implied about THE FOUNDER who intends tight tuning, and this mechanism holds for every founder alike, including Kunert, who 'leaves the minor third near where the casting put it', so the option separates nothing; and 'Every partial in the bell' reaches past the tuners' five, since what a listener hears is 'something the ear assembles out of the upper partials', which nobody turns. The key is the inference that follows specifically from the intent -- 'That one-way arrow is why founders cast heavy', 'carrying an allowance of metal -- twelve kilos on the Cawden bell, against a finished weight of two hundred and twenty-eight -- that exists only to be turned away', and 'They would meet it four kilos apart at the pour'. Key support is stronger than the distractor case; not a double key.

findings.quote: Bats use it in most summers, although it sits in the same position as the laundry's row.
findings.note: PARTIALLY, blind pick C (~70%). A and C form an absolute/qualified minimal pair ('occupied every single summer' vs 'use it in most summers') and the qualified member wins on the usual test-wise heuristic, while B and D are unanchored calendar detail. The tell is probabilistic, not determinative, so flag.

findings.quote: One end of a void was far warmer than the other, and the animals moved between the two.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick D (~75%). A thermal gradient that lets a colony shift between warm and cool ends is the standard roost-ecology fact and the standard explanation for why replacement boxes fail; A additionally falls to 'the whole of a void'. Distractors are substantive, so adjudication rather than kill.

findings.quote: Why some purpose-built replacement roosts are taken up by bats while others stand empty.
findings.note: PARTIALLY, blind pick B (~85%). Main-idea umbrella tell: B covers the whole trial while A, C and D each name a peripheral thread (planning conditions, one officer's method, an inter-officer dispute).

findings.quote: One end of a void was far warmer than the other, and the animals moved between the two.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick D. Thermal gradient within a roost and animals shifting between warm and cool ends is the standard finding in bat-roost literature and the premise the rest of the sheet needs; A ('The whole of a void stayed close to thirty degrees') reads as its purpose-built foil. B is substantively plausible and the item is genuine comprehension work, so flag not kill.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3: wrong verb for the act described. Boxes are put up / fitted / hung — the passage itself uses 'went up', 'fitted between September and February', 'hang the finest box' — and nothing in the text has boxes sealed and later unsealed, so 'opened' is an unmotivated switch that briefly obscures the sense. Editor's rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July'.

findings.quote: the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees
findings.note: class 3: collocation. 'Stand' in the sense of registering a level takes 'at' and a reading, not a space, as subject ('the temperature stands at thirty degrees'). Editor's rewrite: 'the space near the ridge can reach close to thirty degrees'.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3 (idiom/collocation): a bat box is fitted, hung or put up, not 'opened' - the verb belongs to buildings and services, not to a wall-mounted box. The passage itself uses the right verb two sentences later ('those fitted between September and February') and elsewhere ('all fitted out of season', 'You can hang the finest box in the county'), so the slip is visible on the page. editor's rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been fitted in June or July'.

findings.quote: the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees
findings.note: class 2 (preposition choice): a reading stands AT a figure; with the preposition dropped the space appears to 'stand' a temperature rather than register one. editor's rewrite: 'the space near the ridge can stand at close to thirty degrees'.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3 idiom/collocation: bat boxes are put up, fitted or hung, not 'opened' — and the passage's own vocabulary elsewhere is 'went up', 'fitted between September and February', 'hang the finest box', so the one-off verb reads as a slip. Editor's rewrite: 'had been put up in June or July'.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3 idiom/collocation: a bat box is put up, fitted, hung or erected - it is never 'opened'. The piece uses the right verbs everywhere else ('they went up', 'those fitted between September and February', 'You can hang the finest box in the county'), so the odd verb reads as a slip rather than variation. Editor's rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July'

findings.quote: the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees
findings.note: class 3: 'stand' in the temperature sense governs 'at' ('the mercury stood at thirty'); with 'the space' as subject the preposition is dropped and the verb reads bare. Rewrite: 'the space near the ridge can stand at close to thirty degrees'.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3: bat boxes are put up or fitted, not 'opened', and the next sentence uses the right verb ('those fitted between September and February'), so the inconsistency is visible within the paragraph. Rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July'.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3: collocation miss - a bat box is fitted, hung or put up, not 'opened' (buildings and exhibitions open; boxes do not). The passage itself uses the right verbs everywhere else ('those fitted between September and February', 'twenty-four boxes went up on nine buildings', 'You can hang the finest box in the county'), so the outlier reads as a slip rather than a choice. Editor's rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July'.

findings.quote: the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees
findings.note: class 3: 'stand' before a figure normally takes 'at' ('the temperature stood at thirty degrees'), and with 'the space' as subject against the parallel clause's 'sits ten or twelve degrees below it' the bare 'stand close to' reads clipped. Editor's rewrite: 'the space near the ridge can sit at close to thirty degrees'.

findings.quote: Luft tränger in, veden brinner upp i stället för att förkolna, och kolningen går förlorad.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick B (~88%). The defining fact about a charcoal kiln is that air ingress turns pyrolysis into combustion; anyone who knows what kolning is answers without reading a word. A is physically backwards (air makes the mila hotter, not slower to cool) and D falls to 'ofelbart'. Comprehension value is thin here — strong flag, close to the recall boundary, but the mechanism is domain knowledge rather than form, so not a kill.

findings.quote: Kolet smulades sönder vid omlastning och måste fram kort väg, medan tjäran tålde långa transporter.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick D (~85%). Standard economic-history fact: charcoal is friable and bulky so it had to be produced near the hytta, while tar travelled in barrels; A is the straight inversion of that. A passage would ground it, but a domain reader needs none.

findings.quote: Att gränsen kan visa var brukets egen skog tog slut, inte hur långt vinterns slädar kom.
findings.note: PARTIALLY, blind pick A (~68%). A has the canonical shape of a scholarly objection (an alternative explanation for the same boundary), C falls to 'aldrig', and D is a units nitpick that does not bear on the boundary claim. Not decided blind — B remains a live reading — so adjudication.

findings.quote: Luft tränger in, veden brinner upp i stället för att förkolna, och kolningen går förlorad.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE shading into general recall, blind pick B: air ingress turning pyrolysis into combustion is the defining fact about a charcoal kiln and is decidable with no text at all. D is an absolute foil ('ofelbart ... oavsett'). A and C stay plausible enough that the key is not left alone in the plausible set, so flag rather than a RECALL_ONLY kill - but this is the weakest passage-dependence in the unit.

findings.quote: Kolet smulades sönder vid omlastning och måste fram kort väg, medan tjäran tålde långa transporter.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick D: charcoal friability versus barrelled tar is the textbook reason and needs no passage. Aggravating factor for adjudication: the stem sheet itself supplies the fact, since q:1 option C states 'Kolet blir ofta sprött och smulas sönder redan vid den första omlastningen på brukets slädar', so a solver working the sheet in order can corroborate D without reading the text.

findings.quote: motsvarar ungefär vad ett hästekipage hann fram och tillbaka under en kort vinterdag utan att lasta om
findings.note: class 6: 'hinna' takes a complement of distance only loosely here; 'vad ... hann fram och tillbaka' as a measure phrase is clipped and makes the reader reparse. Native alternative: 'motsvarar ungefar hur langt ett hastekipage hann fram och tillbaka under en kort vinterdag' or '... vad ett hastekipage hann med fram och tillbaka ...'

findings.quote: Kolet smulades sönder vid omlastning och måste fram kort väg
findings.note: class 6 (option text, q2 D): 'fram kort vag' as a bare distance adverbial is over-compressed; 'ha kort vag' is idiomatic but 'foras/maste fram kort vag' is not a standing collocation. Native alternative: 'maste fram en kort stracka' or 'kunde bara foras korta strackor'

findings.quote: motsvarar ungefär vad ett hästekipage hann fram och tillbaka under en kort vinterdag utan att lasta om
findings.note: class 6: measure ellipsis — the distance noun is left implicit, so 'vad ... hann fram och tillbaka' forces a reparse (and blurs one-way vs round trip). Native alternative: 'hur långt ett hästekipage hann fram och tillbaka under en kort vinterdag' or 'vad ett hästekipage hann med fram och tillbaka'.

findings.quote: måste fram kort väg
findings.note: class 6 (q2 option D): bare singular 'kort väg' as a directional measure is over-compressed, especially next to the passage's own idiomatic plural 'föra långa vägar'. Native alternative: 'måste fram en kort sträcka' or 'tålde bara korta transporter'.

findings.quote: ända tills täckningen har lagats om
findings.note: class 6/1: wrong particle verb. The particle 'om' means 'again' (göra om, lägga om, måla om); 'laga om' is not a standard combination, and the sense wanted is 'repaired'/'re-laid'. Reads like a blend of laga (repair) and lägga om (re-lay). Native alternative: 'tills täckningen har lagats' or 'tills täckningen har lagts om'.

findings.quote: måste fram kort väg
findings.note: class 6: bare measure phrase without article; the passage itself writes 'föra långa vägar' but 'fram kort väg' is a collocation miss. Native alternative: 'måste fram en kort sträcka' / 'fram en kort väg'.

findings.quote: sedan stubbveden torkat över våren och älvarna gick höga nog att bära tunnorna
findings.note: class 3/6: tense parallelism breaks inside the same 'sedan'-clause — supine ('torkat') coordinated with preterite ('gick'). Native alternative: 'sedan stubbveden torkat över våren och älvarna gått höga nog att bära tunnorna'.

findings.quote: kunde flottas nedför älven
findings.note: class 6: 'flotta' is the specific Swedish term for driving loose timber downriver (flottning), not for shipping sealed barrels; collocation miss a copy editor would pause on. Native alternative: 'kunde fraktas nedför älven' or 'fördes på båt nedför älven'.

findings.quote: måste fram kort väg
findings.note: class 6 (option Q2 D): the bare measure adverbial 'kort väg' is idiomatic in 'ha kort väg', but reads clipped in this modal-ellipsis passive. Native alternative: 'måste fram en kort sträcka' or 'bara kunde fraktas korta sträckor'.

findings.quote: och måste fram kort väg
findings.note: class 6: bare indefinite singular 'kort väg' as a distance adverbial is not idiomatic; the passage's own idiom is the fixed plural ('gick att föra långa vägar på vatten'), and the option breaks it. Native alternative: 'måste fram korta vägar' or 'måste fram en kort sträcka'.

findings.quote: ända tills täckningen har lagats om
findings.note: class 6: 'laga om' is not an established particle verb for re-sealing a milkiln covering; the phrase blends 'lagats' (repaired) with 'lagts om' (re-laid). Native alternative: 'tills täckningen har lagats' or 'tills täckningen har lagts om'.

findings.quote: och måste fram kort väg
findings.note: class 6: bare indefinite singular 'kort väg' as a distance adverbial is off; the passage's own idiom is the fixed plural ('gick att föra långa vägar på vatten'). Native alternative: 'måste fram korta vägar' or 'måste fram en kort sträcka'.

findings.quote: Låntagaren fick säd och lämnade tillbaka lika mycket vid skörden, jämte ett tillägg på vanligen en åttondel.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick C (~75%). How a Swedish sockenmagasin worked — grain lent in spring, repaid in kind after harvest with a customary one-eighth surcharge — is general agrarian-history knowledge, and A is eliminated because repayment in money defeats the granary's purpose. Institutional recall does much of the work, though the item is still a legitimate detail question.

findings.quote: Kyrkvärden förvarade båda nycklarna och kunde därför öppna magasinet utan att någon annan var närvarande.
findings.note: PARTIALLY, near-structural; blind pick A (~82%). B, C and D all describe the ABSENCE of a safeguard (one keyholder acting alone, bookkeeping deferred to year end, one man answering alone for the accounts) — precisely what a magasinsordning exists to prevent — so they cluster and A stands apart as the only ordinary regulation. The asymmetry is close to visible from form alone; held at flag under the calibration bar, but adjudication should consider escalating.

findings.quote: Att den vilar på sparbankerna fastän bokens egen förteckning visar nedläggningar långt före häradets första sparbank.
findings.note: PARTIALLY, blind pick D (~65%). C is D's overstated twin ('ingen enda av socknarna') and falls to its own absoluteness, leaving D as the internally-evidenced critique a reviewer actually makes. A and B stay live, so the item is not decided blind.

findings.quote: Låntagaren fick säd och lämnade tillbaka lika mycket vid skörden, jämte ett tillägg på vanligen en åttondel.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick C: lending in kind and repayment in kind with a supplement is the standard account of the Swedish sockenmagasin, and A (repayment in money) contradicts the institution's purpose while D describes a mechanism that would not spread any risk. B stays substantive, so flag.

findings.quote: Den som inte betalat tillbaka vid Mikaeli fick stå över utlåningen följande vår.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick A: B, C and D each describe governance an ordinance of this kind exists to forbid (a single key-holder, no entry in the books until year-end, sole responsibility for the accounts), so a reader who knows the two-key convention discards all three and A stands alone. The asymmetry needs domain knowledge to see rather than form alone, so flag rather than a structural kill.

findings.quote: Att han överdriver sparbankernas roll så till den grad att ingen enda av socknarna i boken stöder sambandet.
findings.note: PARTIALLY: C and D are near-twins on the savings-bank point, with C absolutised ('ingen enda') and D the measured, evidence-citing version of the same criticism. That pairing is visible from form alone and pushes a blind solver towards D. A and B survive as distinct criticisms, so the tell narrows the field without deciding it - flag.

findings.quote: Roligast att läsa är annars de partier som inte tjänar något argument alls.

findings.note: class 6 (option text, q3 A): wrong government - Swedish has 'aganderatten till X' or 'agandet av X', not 'agandet till X'; the two collocations are blended. Native alternative: 'gjorde aganderatten till magasinen oklar' or 'gjorde det oklart vem som agde magasinen'

findings.quote: Roligast att läsa är annars de partier som inte tjänar något argument alls.
findings.note: class 2/6: 'tjäna ett argument' is English 'serve an argument' in Swedish clothing — Swedish 'tjäna' collocates with 'syfte', 'sak', 'tes', not 'argument'. Native alternative: 'de partier som inte tjänar något syfte i bevisföringen' or 'som inte är där för argumentets skull'.

findings.quote: trots att den gjorde ägandet till magasinen oklart
findings.note: class 6/4 (q3 option A): wrong government — Swedish has 'äganderätten till X' or 'ägandet av X'; 'ägandet till X' is a blend of the two that a copy editor would not leave standing. Native alternative: 'gjorde äganderätten till magasinen oklar' or 'gjorde det oklart vem som ägde magasinen'.

findings.quote: Men detta står i förbigående, på en dryg sida
findings.note: class 6: one 'nämner/säger något i förbigående'; letting the material itself 'stå i förbigående' stretches the collocation. Native alternative: 'Men detta nämns bara i förbigående'.

findings.quote: trots att den gjorde ägandet till magasinen oklart
findings.note: class 6: wrong preposition government. Swedish takes 'äganderätten till X' or 'ägandet av X'; 'ägandet till X' is not idiomatic. The passage itself solves it correctly ('lämnade oklart vem som egentligen ägde magasinet'), so the option text is the outlier. Native alternative: 'gjorde äganderätten till magasinen oklar' or 'gjorde det oklart vem som ägde magasinen'.

findings.quote: de partier som inte tjänar något argument alls
findings.note: class 6/2: 'tjäna ett argument' reads as an English 'serve an argument' collocation; Swedish 'tjäna' takes 'syfte', 'sak', 'ändamål'. Native alternative: 'de partier som inte tjänar något syfte i argumentationen' / 'som inte driver något argument'.

findings.quote: de partier som inte tjänar något argument alls
findings.note: class 6/2: the fixed Swedish collocation is 'tjäna ett syfte/ändamål'; 'tjäna ett argument' patterns on English 'serve an argument'. Defensible as an essayistic extension, but a copy editor would pause. Native alternative: 'de partier som inte tjänar något syfte i bevisföringen' or 'som inte har med argumentationen att göra'.

findings.quote: de partier som inte tjänar något argument alls
findings.note: class 6/2: 'tjäna ett argument' is a borderline calque of English 'serve an argument'; Swedish collocates 'tjäna ett syfte'. Native alternative: 'de partier som inte ska bevisa något alls' or 'som inte tjänar något syfte i argumentationen'.

findings.quote: Där syns hur noga man tänkt sig saken.
findings.note: class 6: 'tänka sig saken' means 'imagine the matter'; with 'hur noga' the intended sense is 'think through'. Native alternative: 'hur noga man hade tänkt igenom saken'.

findings.quote: de partier som inte tjänar något argument alls
findings.note: class 2/6: 'tjäna ett argument' reads as an English 'serve an argument' calque; Swedish collocates 'tjäna ett syfte'. Native alternative: 'som inte tjänar något syfte' or 'som inte driver något argument'.

findings.quote: trots att den gjorde ägandet till magasinen oklart
findings.note: class 6: 'ägandet till' borrows the preposition from 'äganderätten till'. Native alternative: 'äganderätten till magasinen' or 'ägandet av magasinen'. Taste-level: 'ägandet till' does occur in legal prose.

findings.quote: De hade ett givet mått i fyrkant, medan tjockleken blev den som vinterns kyla råkade ge.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick C (~85%). Lake ice can be sawn to a chosen square plan but its thickness is whatever the winter froze — plain physical logic, and A is the exact inversion of it while B is self-undermining ('vägde alltid omkring hundrafemtio kilo, oavsett'). A reader who thinks about how ice was harvested does not need the passage.

findings.quote: De hade ett givet mått i fyrkant, medan tjockleken blev den som vinterns kyla råkade ge.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick C: lake-ice thickness is set by the winter, so harvested blocks are cut to a standard plan measure with the thickness left to the season. A is the physical inverse of that and B is close to self-refuting ('vägde alltid omkring hundrafemtio kilo, oavsett hur kall vintern hade varit'). D remains a substantive detail a passage could carry, so flag.

findings.quote: fyllde det tre vintrar i rad med is från Sävlången
findings.note: class 3: the prepositional object is stranded after the duration adverbial, producing a garden-path reading ('i rad med is'). Native alternative: 'fyllde det med is från Sävlången tre vintrar i rad'.

findings.quote: Huset stod kvar till 1968 och revs för en badplats.
findings.note: class 6: 'revs för en badplats' is compressed; 'riva för' does not carry the purpose sense on its own. Native alternative: 'revs för att ge plats åt en badplats'.
